---
title: "Open labs"
---

An open lab is an hour spent *trying* something: a tool, a workflow, a way of
working that is hard to picture until you have done it. The objectives are
loose on purpose. The point is the experience, and what you notice.

The format borrows from NYU Langone's Prompt-a-thon, where staff picked a
project from a set of "project cards" and worked through it with a chatbot.
Participants reported more confidence afterwards, whether or not they had
been given sample prompts [@pmid:39042600]. That was a survey after one
event, so it shows the format was liked, not that it taught skills. The
[project cards](https://github.com/smallw03/NYULH-Generative-AI-Prompt-a-thon-Project-Cards)
are public if you want more ideas.

**How they run.** You do them on your own, at any time, from this page. Every
lab is self-contained: it says what you need, it uses free or university tools
in a browser, and it uses made-up material only. Some labs may also run at
Watch and do, the optional hands-on session on Wednesdays, 2 to 3:30 p.m.
Mountain time (see the [syllabus](../course/syllabus.qmd)).

::: {.callout-warning title="No patient information, ever"}
Every lab uses invented patients, public documents, or your own made-up
material. Do not swap in anything from a rotation. Your university ChatGPT Edu
and Copilot accounts are covered for patient care, and these labs are not
patient care.

What counts as patient information, and why taking out the name is not
enough: [the patient information page](../course/patient-information.qmd).
:::

## Hear it, draft it, check it: a scribe from the inside

You will play a clinic visit, turn it into a transcript, have a chatbot draft
the note, and then check the note the way you would at 6:40 p.m. with fourteen
notes to sign.

An ambient scribe works in two steps, and each step makes its own kind of
error. First, speech recognition turns the conversation into a transcript.
Its errors are words *misheard*: one drug name heard as another, or a "no"
dropped. Then a language model writes the note from the transcript. Its
errors are sentences *never said*: fluent lines that read like a normal note
but are not in the visit. This lab shows you both. [The ethics
chapter](../chapters/core-ethics-regulation.qmd) covers who answers for them.

**Time.** About 60 minutes. **You need** your university Microsoft 365 login
(for Word for the web) and your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot login. The
visit is invented. Nothing installs.

Made-up patients only: the visit below is fiction, so do not swap in a visit
you saw on a rotation, and do not record a real patient. [What counts as
patient information](../course/patient-information.qmd).

### The visit

Three speakers: the clinician (C), the patient, Mrs. Ellen Park, 79 (P), and
her daughter (D). Read it at a normal speed, with the pauses and corrections as
written. It takes about three minutes.

```{.script}
C: Good morning, Mrs. Park. What brings you in today?
P: The dizziness. It started Tuesday. No, wait, it was Sunday. Sunday after church.
C: Any chest pain with it?
P: No chest pain. No. And I'm not short of breath.
C: Are you still taking the hydralazine, twenty-five milligrams three times a day?
P: Yes. And I took some of my husband's hydroxyzine for the itching last week.
C: Okay. Anything else changed with your medicines?
P: I stopped the atorvastatin about a month ago. My legs ached.
D: She's been falling, though. Twice this month.
P: I didn't fall. I sat down hard. That's different.
C: Are you checking your sugars at home?
P: Usually around one fifty. Sometimes two fifty in the morning.
C: Let's hold the hydralazine if you're dizzy when you stand,
   check your blood pressure lying and standing today,
   and I'll see you back in two weeks.
D: We can't come back in two weeks. Her grandson's wedding is in Fort Collins.
C: Then three weeks, and call us if the dizziness gets worse.
```

### Part A: record and transcribe (10 minutes)

Two or three of you read the parts. Alone, read all of them and change your
voice a little for each speaker.

1. Open a blank document in **Word for the web** with your university login.
2. Choose **Dictate**, then **Transcribe**, then **Start recording**. Read the
   visit. Stop, and let Word finish the transcript.
3. Copy the transcript into a new document.

If Transcribe is not available in your account, use your phone's voice-memo
app if it makes a transcript. If neither works, skip to Part C and use the
script above as a perfect transcript. You will lose the transcription errors,
but not the drafting ones.

### Part B: what was misheard (5 minutes)

Read the transcript against the script. Mark every place where it differs:
a word misheard, a "no" dropped, a speaker label wrong, a correction lost.
Drug names that sound alike are the first place to look.

### Part C: draft the note (5 minutes)

Paste the transcript into ChatGPT Edu or Copilot, signed in with your
university account, with this prompt:

```
You are an ambient documentation tool in an outpatient clinic.
Write a SOAP progress note from this visit transcript.
Use standard clinical abbreviations.
```

### Part D: check it as if you were signing it (25 minutes)

Go through the note sentence by sentence against the script. Put every problem
in one of five boxes:

| Box | What it means | Which step it came from |
|---|---|---|
| Misheard | The transcript was wrong and the note repeated it | Transcribe |
| Never said | A statement that is not in the visit at all | Summarize |
| Left out | Something said that the note dropped | Summarize |
| Wrong person | Something the daughter said, written as the patient's | Either |
| True but not yours | Correct, but not what you would sign, such as a plan you did not make | Summarize |

Then look hard at four lines: the start of the dizziness, the falls, the two
"-zine" drugs, and the atorvastatin. Those are where this visit was built to
go wrong. If your note gets all four right, compare it with a neighbour's.
The same prompt can give different notes.

**Optional, 10 more minutes.** Run Part C again, but paste the *script* instead
of your transcript. Any error left now cannot be a transcription error. That
shows you what the model adds on its own.

### Part E: one rule (5 minutes)

Write one sentence: the rule you will use to read a scribe's draft before you
sign it. Bring it to your Friday group and compare.

::: {.self-check}
Your transcript has Mrs. Park's words right: she stopped the atorvastatin a
month ago. The note says she "continues atorvastatin". Which step most likely
produced that sentence?

- Record
- Transcribe
- [Summarize]{.correct}

::: {.explain}
The transcript was right, so the error came after it. "Continues
atorvastatin" is a fluent sentence that says what is usual for a patient like
her. A transcription error tends to look like a wrong word. A sentence that
sounds exactly like a normal note, and is false, is the summarizing step's
kind of error.
:::
:::

## Your case in a second tool, and the other three

Part B of [the prompting lab](../chapters/enrichment-prompting-lab.qmd) runs
one made-up case twice in one tool. Here, take the same case and both prompts
to a second tool (for example Copilot if you used ChatGPT Edu) and score it the
same way, about 15 minutes. Then run the bare and structured prompts on the
three cases you did not pick, about 15 minutes each. You will see whether a
trap that one tool caught, another missed, and which kind of trap structure
helps with.

## A study guide that cites its sources

Load a few published papers you chose into Gemini Notebook (formerly
NotebookLM), ask it questions, and
check each answer against the paper it cites. You will see what grounding in
your own sources fixes, and what it does not. Written out in full in [the
grounding chapter](../chapters/enrichment-rag-notebooklm.qmd).

## Ask your own sources: a notebook for this week, next week, and your next rotation

You have read the chapters and heard the talks. This lab is a different way
into the same material. You put a week's chapter and its papers into Gemini
Notebook (formerly NotebookLM), ask them questions, and check each answer
against the passage it cites. It was written for Watch and do on Wednesday,
October 28, 2026, and it works on your own at any time.

Gemini Notebook answers from the documents you give it, and each sentence of
an answer links to the passage it came from. [The grounding
chapter](../chapters/enrichment-rag-notebooklm.qmd) explains how that works,
and what it does not fix. This lab is the practice. It ends with the part you
will use after the course: a notebook of your own, for any question where the
answer has to come from sources you chose.

**Time.** About 75 minutes. **You need** a personal Gmail account. Gemini
Notebook does not work with CU credentials, so sign in with Gmail, not your
university login. Making a new Google account may ask for a phone number.
Your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot account in a second tab is optional,
for Part C. Nothing installs.

No patient information. Every source here is a published paper or a chapter
of this book. A personal Gmail account is not covered for patient care, so
nothing from a rotation goes into a notebook, as a source or in a question.
[What counts as patient information](../course/patient-information.qmd).

### Part A: build a notebook (15 minutes)

Choose one of the two source sets below. Week 3 uses the papers from the
October 28 talk on how patients, the public, and physicians see AI. Week 4
uses next week's chapters, so it is also a way to preview them.

1. Open [notebook.google](https://notebook.google/), sign in with your Gmail
   account, and create a new notebook.
2. Add each source in your set. For a paper, open its PMC page, download the
   PDF, and upload it. A PDF brings in the whole paper, tables included. For a
   chapter of this book, add its web address as a website source. If a chapter
   does not import, open it, select all the text, copy it, and add it as
   copied text.
3. Open each source in the notebook and check that the whole text is there.

**Week 3: how patients, the public, and physicians see AI**

| Source | What it is |
|---|---|
| [Talking to patients about AI](../chapters/core-patient-communication.qmd), this book | The week 3 core chapter. Web address: `https://aim.seandavis.net/chapters/core-patient-communication.html` |
| Cavalier et al., *JAMA Network Open*, 2025 [@pmid:40067301]; [PMC11897835](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11897835/) | A survey of 1,455 members of a Duke patient advisory panel. Replies were drafted by AI or by a person, with and without saying which |
| Owens et al., *JAMA Network Open*, 2026 [@pmid:42412426]; [PMC13343239](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13343239/) | Interviews with 40 of those patients about AI-drafted portal messages |
| Busch et al., *JAMA Network Open*, 2025 [@pmid:40493367]; [PMC12152705](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12152705/) | A survey of 13,806 hospital patients at 74 hospitals in 43 countries |
| Saasouh et al., *Frontiers in Anesthesiology*, 2025 [@doi:10.3389/fanes.2025.1676819]; [full text](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/anesthesiology/articles/10.3389/fanes.2025.1676819/full) | An online survey of 382 physicians and 760 patients in the United States |

: Week 3 sources. These studies asked different people in different ways, so keep track of who was asked. {tbl-colwidths="[45,55]"}

**Week 4: who gains from a scribe, who pays, and who answers for it**

| Source | What it is |
|---|---|
| [Ethics: what you owe when you sign the note](../chapters/core-ethics-regulation.qmd), this book | The week 4 core chapter. Web address: `https://aim.seandavis.net/chapters/core-ethics-regulation.html` |
| [Will AI take your job?](../chapters/enrichment-workforce-economics.qmd), this book | A week 4 menu chapter. Web address: `https://aim.seandavis.net/chapters/enrichment-workforce-economics.html` |
| [What AI costs the planet](../chapters/enrichment-environment.qmd), this book | A week 4 menu chapter. Web address: `https://aim.seandavis.net/chapters/enrichment-environment.html` |
| Rotenstein et al., *JAMA*, 2026 [@pmid:41920565]; [PMC13044793](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13044793/) | 8,581 clinicians at five academic health systems: what changed in EHR time and visits after scribe adoption |
| Lukac et al., *NEJM AI*, 2025 [@pmid:41497288]; [PMC12768499](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12768499/) | A randomized trial of two scribe products in 238 outpatient physicians |
| Elsworth et al., 2025; [arXiv 2508.15734](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15734) | Google's own measurement of the energy and water used by one Gemini text prompt |

: Week 4 sources. Three chapters, two scribe studies, and one report from the company that makes the model. {tbl-colwidths="[45,55]"}

### Part B: ask, then check three sentences (20 minutes)

Start with a question the sources can answer. Paste the prompt for your set
into the chat.

Week 3:

```
Using only these sources, where do patients and physicians agree about AI in
patient care, and where do they disagree? For each point, say which study it
comes from, who was asked, and how they were asked.
```

Week 4:

```
Using only these sources, should a hospital adopt an ambient AI scribe?
Separate what the studies measured from what they did not measure.
Say who produced each number.
```

Most of a good answer is right. Your job is to find out which parts. Pick
three sentences that matter: a number, a claim about "patients" or
"physicians" in general, and anything that surprised you. Check each one the
way the grounding chapter shows: click the citation, read a line above and a
line below, and ask whether the sentence is narrower or broader than the
passage.

| Sentence | Source and passage | Your call |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | | Supported / broader than the source / not in the source |
| 2 | | Supported / broader than the source / not in the source |
| 3 | | Supported / broader than the source / not in the source |

::: {.self-check}
A notebook writes: "A large international survey found that patients trust AI
in health care." The citation opens a real passage in Busch et al.: 57.6% of
respondents had a positive general view of AI in health care. What is wrong
with the sentence?

- The citation was made up
- [The sentence is broader than the study]{.correct}
- Nothing: the passage supports it

::: {.explain}
The passage is real and the number is right. But the same abstract says
"fewer than half of the participants expressed positive attitudes regarding
all items pertaining to trust in AI", and 72.9% preferred decisions led by a
physician, even if that meant slightly lower accuracy. A positive general view
is not trust. These were also hospital patients who chose to answer, not
patients in general. Nothing was invented, and only reading the passage shows
what is wrong.
:::
:::

### Part C: ask what the sources cannot answer (10 minutes)

Now ask a question your sources do not cover.

- Week 3: *How do patients at CU Anschutz feel about AI-drafted portal
  messages?*
- Week 4: *What would an ambient scribe cost our hospital per clinician per
  year, and what is its carbon footprint?*

The notebook may say the sources do not answer this, which is the right
answer. If it gives an answer anyway, click its citations. Is each number in a
source, or was it put together from pieces? Then ask the same question in
ChatGPT Edu or Copilot. It can search the web, so it may find something. If it
does, where did the answer come from, and would you repeat it to a colleague?

### Part D: make something you will use (15 minutes)

The Studio panel turns your sources into other forms: a study guide,
flashcards, a quiz, a mind map, a slide deck, an infographic, or an Audio
Overview, which is a podcast-style conversation about the sources. Make one
you will use this week.

- Week 3: flashcards or a quiz, before Friday's small group, where you bring
  clinical stories.
- Week 4: an Audio Overview of next week's chapters, to listen to before
  Monday's talk.

Most outputs let you add your own instructions before you generate. Say who it
is for and what it must keep, for example: *for a fourth-year medical student;
say who was asked in each study; do not generalize beyond them.* A Video
Overview can take more than 30 minutes to generate ([Google: Video
Overviews](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/16454555)), so
leave that one for later.

Do not count on a Studio output to link each sentence to its passage, the way
a chat answer does. Pick one claim from what you made, and find it in the
sources yourself.

### Part E: your own notebook (10 minutes)

The routine you just used works for any question where the answer has to come
from documents you chose, and not from whatever a chatbot finds on the web.
Some places it fits in the next year:

- A guideline for your next rotation. Load the guideline, the evidence review
  behind it, a guideline from another organization, and a patient handout,
  then ask where they disagree and which is newer. For breast cancer screening
  that is the USPSTF recommendation [@pmid:38687503], its evidence review
  [@pmid:38687490], the American Cancer Society guideline [@pmid:26501536],
  which starts at a different age and is nine years older, and the [NCI
  patient summary](https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/patient/breast-screening-pdq).
- This week's [Learn it with AI](../course/learn-with-ai.qmd) topic: the
  papers and notes you are learning from.
- A drug you prescribe often: its FDA label from
  [DailyMed](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/) and the trial that led to
  its approval.
- Your own notes: a lecture or a review sheet you wrote, turned into a quiz.
- A residency program's published curriculum or handbook, before an interview
  or before your first day.

Use a chatbot with web search instead when you do not have the sources yet. A
notebook is not a literature search: it only knows what you put in it. And
patient information never goes into a notebook on a personal account.

Write one sentence: a task you will use a notebook for in the next month, and
the three to five sources you would put in it. Bring it to your Friday group.

### Keep it

Your notebook stays in your Google account. Keep the three sentences you
checked, and the task you wrote down.

## Build a calculator, then break it

Describe a clinical score to an AI app builder and have it build a working
calculator in the browser. Then try to break it with made-up patients at the
edges. You will see how fast a tool appears, and how hard it is to know
whether it is right. Written out in full in [the agentic coding
chapter](../chapters/enrichment-agentic-coding.qmd).

## Draw me a doctor

*Idea.* Ask an image generator for "a doctor", "a nurse", "a surgeon", "a
patient with a rash". Make twenty of each and count what you see: age, sex,
skin tone, setting. Compare with real workforce numbers. Connects to [bias and
equity](../chapters/core-bias-equity.qmd).

## The patient who talks back

*Ready.* The full lab is [Part B of talking to
patients](../chapters/core-patient-communication.qmd#part-b-practice-patient):
a chatbot plays a patient who brings a chatbot's printout, you play the doctor,
and then it scores you as an observer. In the open lab, run that, then change
the patient to another hard conversation: a new cancer diagnosis, a medication
error, a patient who wants antibiotics for a cold. [NYU Grossman's Prompt-a-Thon library](https://promptathon.iime.cloud/)
has virtual-patient prompts to start from; copy them into your university
ChatGPT Edu or Copilot.

## Deep research, checked

*Idea.* Run a "deep research" query on a narrow clinical question. Then check
every citation in the report: does the paper exist, does it say that, is it
the best evidence? Connects to [critical
appraisal](../chapters/core-appraisal.qmd).

## Teach a machine in ten minutes

*Idea.* Train an image classifier in your browser with a free tool and your
webcam: two classes, a few dozen pictures each. Then change the lighting, the
background, or the person, and watch it fail. Connects to [how these systems
work](../chapters/core-foundations.qmd).

## A handout your patient can read

*Idea.* Take a public patient handout, ask a chatbot to rewrite it at a sixth-
grade reading level and then translate it into Spanish. Translate it back and
compare. What changed, and what would a patient now misunderstand? Connects to
[talking to patients](../chapters/core-patient-communication.qmd).

## Write your own board question

*Idea.* Ask a chatbot to write five exam-style multiple-choice questions on a
topic you are studying. Then check each one against a real source: is the
keyed answer right, is each wrong option clearly wrong, and would the question
teach anything? [NYU Grossman's Prompt-a-Thon library](https://promptathon.iime.cloud/) has question-writing prompts to start from. Connects to
[critical appraisal](../chapters/core-appraisal.qmd).

## Build the tool you wish existed

*Idea.* Think of a small tool you wish you had on a rotation: a page of the
formulas you use every day, discharge instructions matched to a patient's
reading level, a sign-up page for a clinic project. Describe it in plain
English to an AI app builder and see how far you get in an hour. Then ask what
you would need to check before anyone used it. The open-ended version of
[build a calculator, then break
it](#build-a-calculator-then-break-it); connects to [the agentic coding
chapter](../chapters/enrichment-agentic-coding.qmd).

## Ask questions of a dataset

*Idea.* Open a public health dataset in Google Colab, a free notebook that
runs in the browser, and ask its built-in AI assistant to answer questions in
plain English: how many, how has it changed, is this group different? It
writes and runs the code. Then check one answer by hand, and ask whether the
question was a fair one for the data. Connects to [how these systems
work](../chapters/core-foundations.qmd).
